Finding the Tailwinds That Help Us Move Forward

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

So often, our attention gravitates toward what is wrong, challenging, or missing. Yet when we focus solely on what is not working, we lose sight of the things that are helping us along.

I find it helpful to think about the headwinds and tailwinds moving through our lives.

Headwinds are the pressures, stressors, and challenges that push against us. They are the things coming at us, demanding our attention, threatening to knock us off course, or making it harder to move in the direction we want to go. Some are temporary, while others are part of circumstances we cannot quickly change. Tailwinds are the forces supporting us from behind and within. They include our strengths, skills, relationships, routines, experiences, and values that help us keep going. They may not remove the headwinds, but they can help us meet them with greater support and perspective.

In Stress Wisely, I explore wellness through eight interconnected dimensions: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, environmental, occupational, financial, and spiritual. Each offers a different lens through which we're able to notice what is hindering us, what is helping us, and where we might find room for growth.

Wellness is an ongoing process of understanding what we need, noticing what supports us, and making adjustments as our circumstances change. Perhaps we are not sleeping as well as we would like, feel disconnected from the people we care about, are carrying financial stress, or have lost touch with the activities that give our lives meaning. These concerns deserve our attention, and sometimes they call for change, additional support, or a closer look at what is possible within our circumstances. At the same time, my gentle invitation is to ask ourselves: What is already working for me here?

It is easy to focus on what our bodies are not able to do or what we wish we could change, but we can also appreciate what they help us experience and what we are doing to care for them. Perhaps a 30-minute walk every day helps you clear your mind, a consistent bedtime is allowing you to show up with better energy, or you've learned to recognize when you are running on empty and need to slow down. These everyday choices matter.

If you thought of your body as a vehicle carrying you through life, what is helping you take good care of it and keep it going?

Emotional wellness is about learning to recognize our feelings and respond to them with greater understanding instead of ignoring them or expecting ourselves to push through them. One tailwind may be your growing ability to name what you are feeling. Maybe you give yourself 90 seconds to sit with an emotion and let it move through you, find comfort in a creative outlet, or reach out to a trusted person rather than carrying everything alone. These are ways of making room for our emotions as we navigate the hard parts.

What helps you process your feelings and meet yourself with a little more compassion?

We learn through curiosity, reflection, conversation, and experience. Each and every one of us has skills we've developed over time, mistakes we've learned from, and different perspectives we've opened ourselves up to that have broadened our thinking.

Thinking of a particular area in your life, what have you learned, figured out, or become more capable of doing?

We are not meant to navigate life alone. A friend who checks in, a colleague who understands, or a community where we feel we belong can remind us we are supported and valued. We can also notice the strengths we bring to our relationships, such as being a good listener, a thoughtful encourager, or a practical problem-solver. Connection is about the support we receive, but it's also about the ways we contribute to one another.

Who helps you feel safe, seen, and supported? What do you bring to the relationships that matter to you?

Our surroundings can influence how we feel and move through our days. We can't always change our environment, but we can notice the places that bring a little ease. Maybe it's a favourite park bench, a sunny spot by your living room window, or a calm corner where you can collect your thoughts. Creating and spending time in hope-filled havens that offer comfort and inspiration can make a difference.

Which places help you feel more settled, connected, or at ease?

Our contributions extend beyond paid work to include caregiving, parenting, volunteering, and the many responsibilities that make up our days. When the demands feel relentless, we may overlook the care we bring to our work, the problems we have solved, or the difference we make in the lives of others. A tailwind might be recognizing a task you carry out that makes someone else's day easier, setting a boundary around email, asking for support, keeping a commitment that reflects your values, or celebrating the small wins.

Where do you find meaning in the work you get to do, and what helps you do it in a sustainable way?

When financial pressures are weighing on us, it can be hard to see what we're doing well and what is working for us. Recognizing what's helping us doesn't mean pretending those worries aren't real. Perhaps you have become more aware of your spending, started a conversation you've been avoiding, learned something about budgeting, or reached out to understand your options.

What is helping you feel more informed, supported, or prepared when it comes to your resources?

Spiritual wellness can be rooted in faith, and it can also be found in our values, sense of purpose, and connection to something larger than ourselves. Noticing the moments that remind us of what matters most can help us make choices that reflect it. Maybe it's spending time in nature, being of service, a prayer practice or familiar ritual, or making time for the people and causes you care about.

When do you feel most connected to what matters most to you?

We cannot always choose what life brings our way. Yet even when things feel difficult, we can widen our view so that what is hard is not the only thing we see.

This is where I believe gratitude is one of the mightiest forces we have for living well. It draws our attention to what might otherwise go unnoticed, helping us recognize what is sustaining us today and what we can carry forward into tomorrow.

Hanley-Dafoe, R. (2023). Stress wisely: How to be well in an unwell world. Page Two.

The Patient Voice Was Invited Into the Room. Was It Heard?

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Something has been bothering me since I spoke at a cardiology conference this summer.

The invitation felt significant. As both a psychologist and someone whose life has depended on cardiology since infancy, I was honoured to be part of a symposium alongside several highly respected professors. I arrived feeling optimistic.

For most of my life, congenital heart disease was viewed largely through a biomedical lens. Survival was the priority. While this has begun to change, I left the conference wondering how far we have really come.

Walking through the exhibition hall, I was struck by the advances in technology and clinical care. Yet as the day went on, I found myself thinking less about conditions and treatments and more about the people living through them.

One interaction stayed with me. Hoping to discuss patient experience, I approached a heart charity's stand. Staff appeared busy filming promotional content for social media. Perhaps I arrived at the wrong moment, but it felt symbolic: considerable attention devoted to communicating about patients, less directed toward listening to them.

The exhibition hall was unexpectedly triggering. Surrounded by equipment and technology, I was transported back to the hospitals of my childhood and had to step outside to ground myself. Yet these were not simply memories from a distant past. As someone who still lives with congenital heart disease and depends on ongoing specialist care, the world I was walking through was also part of my present and future.

Although I attended as a psychologist and researcher, I was also there as a patient. I have experienced recent setbacks in my cardiac health and am currently off work while trialling one of the medications discussed during the symposium.

The other presentations focused on highly technical aspects of cardiac care. I was discussing the psychological experience of living with congenital heart disease and a lifetime of medical intervention. I spent longer than usual on my own story because I wanted the audience to see healthcare through the eyes of a child receiving it.

As I spoke, several people left. They may have had other commitments, but the moment stayed with me because it echoed a question that had been growing throughout the day: What happens when discussion turns from disease to lived experience?

Later, I described childhood pacemaker checks: lying dizzy and breathless on a hospital bed while clinicians learned to use emerging technology, gripping my mother's hand and counting holes in ceiling tiles. A small ripple of laughter spread through the audience. I suspect people were responding to how much technology has changed. Yet I found myself wondering whether we had taken away the same story. I was describing what it felt like to be the child on the bed.

The final troubling moment came at the end of the session. Several speakers had overrun, and there was no time for questions after my presentation. Perhaps it was simply unfortunate timing, yet I could not ignore the symbolism. The one presentation focused on lived experience was the one that never became a conversation.

Perhaps part of what stayed with me was the contrast with psychology conferences, where lived experience often sits at the centre of discussion. These topics usually generate deep engagement and reflection. Their relative absence on this occasion left me wondering whether healthcare still finds it easier to engage with what can be measured and treated than with what it feels like to live through those experiences.

On the train home, I found myself thinking about the child I once was and the many children I had known on cardiac wards over the years—the ones lying in hospital beds while adults discussed conditions, procedures, and outcomes over their heads.

This is not a criticism of individual clinicians, many of whom are passionate advocates for psychologically informed care. Rather, it left me reflecting on a wider culture within healthcare. Even among deeply caring professionals, it can sometimes feel easier to discuss disease than lived experience.

I was also struck by how little attention was paid to the psychological well-being of healthcare professionals themselves. There was little discussion of burnout, compassion fatigue, vicarious trauma, or moral injury, despite these being well-recognised occupational risks.

Modern medicine has become remarkably effective at helping people survive. Understanding survival, however, is not the same as understanding what survival feels like.

The day also forced me to confront something I often overlook: the personal cost of repeatedly turning my own medical history into a teaching tool.

For years, I have shared my story in the hope of helping healthcare become more psychologically informed. Yet congenital heart disease is not a chapter of my life that ended in childhood. It is a lifelong condition that continues to shape my health, identity, and future. As someone who still depends on specialist cardiac care, I am never speaking solely about the past.

Looking after my own mental health is not separate from that work. It is what allows me to continue doing it.

As someone who has lived with congenital heart disease my entire life, I know how much has changed. When I was a child, survival was often the only conversation. Today, we know far more about the psychological realities of living with lifelong conditions and the importance of supporting patients, families, and healthcare professionals.

The evidence is there, yet psychologically informed care can still feel confined to a dedicated session or token talk rather than something embedded throughout healthcare. Patient experience should not be an optional addition to discussions of treatment and outcomes. It should help shape them.

Morton, L. (2026). Beyond the Medical Gaze: Practicing Psychologically Informed Healthcare. Oxford University Press.

Who Am I Minus My Spouse?

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Not that I ever gave any thought to being widowed before it happened, but if I had, I probably would not have understood to what extent it would involve figuring out who I am.

I still don’t know how to be out in this world without the cloak of marriage between me and me.

I’m just kind of stumbling around, figuring out what I do because it’s what we did and what we did because it was what I liked to do. What to keep from my past life, what to let go, what to add. I can’t be the person I was before Tom because that person was in her 20s. I’ve only ever been an adult side-by-side with Tom. Now, suddenly, I’m figuring out what I like to eat. (Back in the day it was bacon cheeseburgers all the time. Not so much now.) Where I like to go. Who I like to hang out with. What I want to watch or listen to. Music was life for Tom, so that's what we listened to any time the TV wasn't on. He was in charge of choosing, always respectful of where our tastes differed. Now I feel disloyal on the days I listen to talk radio instead.

Weirdest of all, I’m single. Do I want to stay that way or try to date? At my age? At the moment the thought does not appeal, but I sure feel exposed and vulnerable walking around all unattached. I feel—embarrassing to say this—invalidated. (I know, I know...that's not only wrong but also insulting to all the other single people in the world. But it's just how I feel about me. You all are great.) When Tom went, he took part of my identity with him.

The social world in which Tom and I circulated has, to a great extent, dissipated. Mick Jagger notwithstanding, rock ‘n’ roll has a shelf life, and as my peers and I move through our 60s, we indulge in fewer loud, late nights. Musician friends have retired, moved away, passed away. So in some ways, life would be different even if Tom were still around.

But it would be different with Tom, meaning much of it would be the same. Comfy and well-worn. We’d go out to eat, hang with friends, see live music. We’d take road trips. Visit family. We’d sit on the couch after dinner and watch TV and Tom would fall asleep and I would be annoyed, but that was life and it was dear.

Now even the familiar is different. I live in the same house and sleep in the same bed, but there's a big empty space in both. I have coffee every morning but make it myself instead of having it brought to me in bed. (He was an early riser, I'm not.) I still eat dinner every night, but not at the same time and not the same kind of meals; they might not be the meat, starch, veggie Tom insisted on. Some nights they're just chips and salsa (starch and veggie). I still watch TV on the couch after dinner but now dogs sleep next to me.

I eat out and see live music a lot less often because if I don’t want to go alone, both require a level of proactivity I don’t always feel up to. It was a whole lot easier to just turn to Tom and make a suggestion than it is to figure out who to call, get in touch, hope they’re free and interested, make a plan, and follow through. And now, instead of just riding along on what Tom wants to do sometimes, I alone am responsible for keeping myself entertained. It's a lot of work and more than once I've done things I thought I would like but it turned out I didn't.

I try to stay busy, saying yes to most invitations—it’s a couples’ world so I don’t get many—hoping to enjoy myself. I don’t always have fun, but I give it a shot. I go out alone with varying degrees of success, sometimes arriving at an event and leaving immediately, other times sticking around but so awkwardly that I berate myself for days after, wishing Tom were around because just the fact that he loved me was enough to make feel like less of a loser. Sometimes the stars align and I have fun and don’t do anything cringe. This feels like an accomplishment.

Of course it’s not all bad. Fortunately, as an introvert, I’m good at being alone. This past summer I loaded up the dogs and drove to the Oregon coast, where we spent a month. I took long walks on the beach, read, painted, hiked, and watched old movies. Were Tom still alive this would have been impossible because he had a business to tend (my work is portable), so it was something new and wonderful just for me and my dogs. (My dogs, never ours. That feels strange in itself.) I was sometimes lonely but mostly content. I hope to do it again next year.

But now I’m back home, negotiating a life that resembles my old life, but is very different. I haven’t felt this awkward in my own skin since I was a teenager.

I spent most of my life in a we and now, suddenly, it’s just me.

A Flawed Study Shaped the Treatment of Childhood Depression

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Can one bad apple spoil the entire bushel?

In science, a single flawed study can sometimes distort a larger body of evidence. A recent report, “Prozac use for childhood depression skewed by single flawed medical trial,” describes how one clinical trial may have influenced a major synthesis of research—and, in turn, prescribing practices for children with depression.(1)

In the recent review, a central question for researchers was: “How well does Prozac work for children with depression, compared with other treatments?” When many clinical trials point in the same direction, pediatricians and mental health professionals take notice. Whatever one’s view of medicating children for conditions such as attention-deficit disorders, anxiety, or depression, everyone should want prescribing decisions to rest on sound evidence. In this case, however, a single trial conducted in Iran with only 40 patients appeared to have had an outsized impact on the evaluation of using Prozac—fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)—to treat pediatric depression.

Here is what happened. A meta-analysis combined results from multiple studies on this question. Researchers included several clinical trials comparing Prozac with other treatments, but that single study from Iran, published 20 years ago, produced unusually strong results and exerted a disproportionate effect on the overall analysis. That outlier shifted the findings in favor of Prozac, helping to shape the message that Prozac was especially effective and preferred for treating depressed children. The concern is not that this medication necessarily caused unusual harm or side effects, but that clinicians may have been misled and made treatment decisions using flawed evidence that was less conclusive than it looked.

This case highlights a broader truth about how science works and how research is used to validate treatments. Anecdotes can be compelling, but they are not the same as scientific evidence. Personal stories may raise important questions, yet they have not been tested through systematic methods. One data point does not establish a trend.

A familiar example is “vaccine hesitancy.” When public figures elevate anecdotal accounts over tested evidence, the result can be unnecessary illness. For example, when parents decline the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine due to unsupported claims linking the vaccine to autism, this frightens parents away from child vaccinations. Information shapes behavior, and this behavior affects the health of an entire community.

Psychology explains why such claims gain traction. Contrarians and independent-minded people may resist broad health mandates when they seem to override individual choices. Yet population health sometimes depends on widespread participation in behaviors—such as vaccination or masking during an outbreak—that reduce risks not only for individuals but also for those around them. Consider the difference between wearing a seat belt and wearing a mask. If one passenger chooses not to wear a seat belt, the consequences may fall primarily on that person. If one infected and contagious person chooses not to wear a mask, others may be exposed, and the illness spreads. Public health asks us to balance individual preferences with the collective risk.

It is easy to forget that the medicines are, in fact, technologies. Researchers also rely on technology to develop the drugs, recruit patients, conduct trials, and analyze results. Artificial intelligence may soon accelerate the design of new molecules and model virtual clinical trials. But no computational shortcut will replace careful procedures or critical thinking. Clinicians must carefully examine a drug treatment’s record of effectiveness and safety. Decisions that affect health cannot be driven by viral memes or anecdotal claims.

In this case, scientists identified the problem, reanalyzed the data, and widely shared the corrected results. Pediatric clinical guidance was revised, and the claim that Prozac is superior for childhood depression now appears less certain. This does not mean clinicians have been told to stop prescribing Prozac to children. Other options are available, but the larger lesson is that science is not about always being right; it is about being willing to look again for errors, and revise conclusions.

We can leave the broader debate about medicating children with depression for another time. For now, the essential point is that we must keep testing—not only new medicines, but also the assumptions that shape how we interpret the evidence. Science depends on our willingness to question our conclusions. This is how science corrects itself and thus serves us better.

Plöderl M, Lyus R, Horowitz M & Moncrieff. (2025). The loss of efficacy of fluoxetine in pediatric depression: explanations, lack of acknowledgment, and implications for other treatments. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 189.

Van Noorden, R. (2026). Prozac use for childhood depression skewed by single flawed medical trial. Nature, NEWS 10/2/2026. nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02769-x

Zhou X, Teng T, Zhang Y et al. (2020). Comparative efficacy and acceptability of antidepressants, psychotherapies, and their combination for acute treatment of children and adolescents with depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. The Lancet Psychiatry, 7, 581-601 thelancet.com/journals/lanpsy/article/PIIS2215-0366(20)30137-1/fulltext

How Moral Injury Worsens Burnout

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated October 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

As someone interested in both morality and human motivation, I’ve found myself thinking recently about the connections between burnout and moral injury. Burnout, as you may have experienced viscerally, is a state of profound exhaustion in which you feel depleted and unmotivated after being too stressed for too long.

Moral injury, meanwhile, often happens when you know the ethical thing to do in a given situation, but can’t do it because you lack resources or support. During the COVID pandemic, doctors and nurses were often unable to treat patients adequately because they ran out of supplies and hospital rooms. And at countless workplaces, people who witness colleagues fudging numbers or cooking the books keep silent, fearing they'll be ostracized if they speak up.

While burnout and moral injury are distinct phenomena, research suggests that not only are they intertwined, but moral injury can actually make burnout worse. In one study, the more morally distressing situations people faced, the more emotional exhaustion they felt, which is a major component of burnout.

Studies like this pass the smell test. For most of us, it’s easy to think of times when witnessing wrongdoing or injustice made getting through the day feel like a struggle. If you feel morally compromised at work, even setting a healthy work pace that balances rest and engagement isn’t going to replenish your energy.

In a recent editorial, American Medical Association past president Bobby Mukkamala argues that burnout and moral injury can’t be solved just on the individual level, by those who are already suffering. Instead, these issues call for systems-level solutions.

I couldn’t agree more, and the good news is that certain systemic changes can strike at the root of both problems. Organizational research suggests that when managers encourage an atmosphere of trust and openness within their teams, people can feel safe speaking up about both moral qualms and mental overload, and team members can solidify practices of helping each other through these challenges so that no one feels isolated or cut off from support.

While writing my book The Art of Pacing, I was lucky enough to observe this kind of culture incubating among Brown University surgeons-in-training. When people feel psychologically safe from the get-go—an atmosphere Brown program leaders have worked to foster—it's easier for them to pace themselves through satisfying, decades-long careers, rather than hitting a mental or moral wall and leaving their chosen work behind.

Mercedes-Benz Is Giving Up On Its EV Charging Network In Europe

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Mercedes-Benz has exited the EV charging market in Europe, selling its network to French operator Electra. The move was disclosed in the automaker’s third-quarter financial report, where the German brand said that the assets associated with the business were valued at €99 million ($111 million).

The sale, first reported by Electrive, means that Mercedes-Benz will now rely on external partnerships for EV charging exclusively in Europe. The car manufacturer’s proprietary EV network had 374 fast-charging ports at 47 locations across the region, all of which are now part of Electra’s growing network.

As part of the transaction, Electra is now a “Premium Partner,” second only to Ionity. What’s more, Mercedes-Benz EV drivers can now charge at discounted rates at over 5,000 Electra chargers across 800 locations in several European countries.

The German automaker’s fast charging business in the United States is unaffected by the European sale. That said, the move shows that Mercedes-Benz is no longer willing to invest its own money into building a premium charging experience. Instead, it’s relying on big partners like Ionity, which is already one of the best-performing networks in Europe.

One reason for the sale may be economies of scale. Paul Tonini, Electra’s General Manager for Germany, told Electrive that the market is increasingly consolidating around larger providers, which means that relatively small players like the now-defunct Mercedes-Benz Charging Network in Europe have a hard time keeping finances in check.

The bigger the network, the larger the potential for income. Meanwhile, Mercedes-Benz gets premium access to the network it used to operate, as it looks to expand its partnerships with third-party providers, offering EV owners discounted rates at more than one network.

The Mercedes-Benz Charging Network launched just three years ago, with a goal of having over 10,000 fast chargers globally by the end of the decade. The company uses high-powered charging equipment from Alpitronic, with the majority of sites having 400-kilowatt dispensers. Earlier this year, the first 1,000-kilowatt-capable stalls were installed at charging parks in Europe and North America.

This past weekend, the former Mercedes-Benz stalls have been integrated into Electra’s network. The card payment terminals will be replaced soon, and the station branding will also be changed to reflect Electra’s ownership.

In the United States, Mercedes-Benz’s High-Power Charging network has 748 charging ports at 80 locations, according to the Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center. Additionally, 62 ports at eight stations are available in Canada.

Three types of chargers can be found on BP Pulse’s network. The lowest-powered stalls are made by Tritium and can deliver up to 150 kW. The company also uses 180 kW ABB dispensers, as well as 400 kW Alpitronic stalls. The smallest BP Pulse stations have just two stalls, while the largest site, located in Inglewood, California, has 48 stalls, according to DCFC Tracker. Pricing on BP Pulse varies between $0.33/kilowatt-hour and $0.65/kilowatt-hour.

Charging networks working better together benefits the entire EV ecosystem and is an important step toward accelerating EV adoption."

Through the ChargeHub app, drivers can find and pay for sessions at over 40 different operators in the United States and Canada. Additionally, another 70+ networks, including Tesla, Ionna, and Electrify America, can be found on ChargeHub.

Nearly 1 In 3 Hyundais Sold In October Was A Hybrid As High Gas Prices Push Buyers To Pivot

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

A whopping 29% of Hyundai’s total October sales volume in the U.S. were hybrids, the automaker said Tuesday. That’s the highest mix ever for gas-electric powertrains for the Korean automaker, thanks to buyers seeking more fuel efficient cars due to gas prices that have remained stubbornly high since the start of the U.S. war in Iran.

Hyundai doesn't break out hybrid sales in its monthly reports, instead bundling them together under individual model names. But it did say that hybrid versions of the Santa Fe and Palisade set new October sales records. Meanwhile, sales of the all-electric Ioniq 5 bounced back, climbing 21% year over year to 1,981 units.

Hyundai sold 73,452 vehicles in October, a 5% increase over the same month last year. Its year-to-date sales now stand at 770,916 units, up 3% from 2025.

Sister brand Kia also reported record overall and electrified vehicle sales. It sold 80,008 vehicles last month, bringing its year-to-date total to 747,394 units, not far behind Hyundai.

Kia's hybrid sales jumped 114% year over year, helped by strong demand for hybrid versions of the popular Sportage and Sorento SUVs and the Carnival minivan. But the more interesting news is the recovery in Kia's EV sales, which have struggled for several quarters.

Sales of the three-row EV9 surged 111% to 1,406 units, while EV6 sales climbed 58% to 803 units. Kia also sold 976 units of the more affordable EV3, whose production and deliveries are still ramping up following its recent U.S. launch.

There's a caveat to those EV growth figures, though. The Ioniq 5, EV6, and EV9 were all coming off a particularly weak October 2025, when sales cratered following the expiration of the federal EV tax credit a month earlier.

The months leading up to the September 2025 deadline saw buyers rush to claim the incentive, pulling demand forward and causing subsequent sales to decline. The broader EV market has been gradually recovering since, with the third quarter marking its strongest performance since then.

The EV3, meanwhile, could give Kia's electric lineup another shot in the arm. Ferrari's first all-electric model is already sold out for 2027, the automaker said during its third-quarter earnings call Tuesday. The Luce starts at an eye-watering $560,800 in the U.S., but neither its price nor its controversial design appears to be putting off Ferrari's deep-pocketed clientele.

“The Luce that we plan to sell next year basically are all allocated,” Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna said in the earnings call. He added that customers placing an order now would have to wait a year to take delivery. Ferrari didn't disclose how many units it plans to sell or provide a regional breakdown of its orders.

Designed through a collaboration with former Apple design chief Jony Ive's LoveFrom, the first electric Prancing Horse looks nothing like the Ferraris we're used to seeing. It trades the brand's signature aggressive, low-slung proportions for a higher-riding silhouette with an industrial-design aesthetic. The Luce is also Ferrari's first-ever five-seat car. The radical departure hasn't gone down particularly well with critics, many of whom have questioned whether the design looks like a Ferrari at all.

Ferrari isn't alone in taking a more unconventional approach to EV design. Jaguar's new Type 01 and the all-electric Mercedes-AMG GT have also sparked plenty of debate. Key rival Lamborghini, meanwhile, has scrapped plans for its first-ever EV, opting to stick with hybrids and gas models for now.

Vigna, however, said buyers were better understanding the Luce after seeing it in person and getting behind the wheel. “We see when and how the perception changes when the people drive the car,” he said.

Early media reviews appear to support that argument. A handful of outlets have already had the opportunity to drive the Luce, and the initial impressions have been overwhelmingly positive. MotorTrend, for instance, described its driving dynamics as “beguilingly natural in its responses, fluid and concise in its change of direction, and beautifully balanced through all phases of a corner.”

The Luce is a beast on paper. It's equipped with quad motors—one at each wheel—for a total of 1,035 horsepower and 730 pound-feet of torque. That's enough to rocket the Luce to 62 mph in 2.5 seconds, Ferrari says. The EV also has rear-wheel steering and a suspension setup derived from the F80 supercar. Steering wheel-mounted paddles let the driver jack up torque or regenerative braking, which is supposed to make the car more engaging to drive.

The EV-specific specs are less impressive for a half-million-dollar car. The Luce's 112-kilowatt-hour battery uses SK On pouch cells and provides 530 kilometers (329 miles) of range on Europe's WLTP cycle. That should translate to somewhere under 300 miles when it gets an EPA rating. Peak charging power lands at 350 kilowatts, which is plenty strong in objective terms but falls short of some of the fastest-charging EVs. But then again, you don't buy a $560,000 Luce because you're looking for a great, practical electric car.

And if there were any doubts about how much wealthy collectors are willing to pay for Ferrari's first EV, consider what happened in August. The first production Luce, dubbed “Chassis 0,” fetched a staggering $40 million at auction, making it the most expensive new car ever sold at auction.

Used EVs Are Selling Like Hotcakes. The Fastest Movers May Surprise You

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Used EVs are getting more popular. Not only are they increasing in popularity, they're selling even faster than their hybrid and even gasoline counterparts, according to iSeeCars.

You might assumed that all of the used Teslas hitting the market would be a big reason why. But in reality, no Tesla even cracked the top 10 list of best-selling used EVs in September 2026.

Compared to the same month last year, this September saw a 9.8% price increase for used EVs. That's exactly double the 4.8% increase used hybrids saw year-over-year. However, both absolutely crush used gas car values, which only jumped 0.3%. You can bet that high fuel prices over the past year or so have had an affect on gas and diesel demand. People are thinking about EVs more than ever before, especially every time the see eye-watering receipts from every fill up.

“These pricing shifts reflect significantly different year-over-year trends across drivetrains,” iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer said in a release. “Ongoing higher fuel prices are likely driving the shift, though the EV segment has also recovered from the demand turbulence caused by the loss of federal incentives a year ago.”

Price isn't the only indicator of demand, though. Speed is another. Used EVs fly off the figurative shelves faster than gas cars, spending an average of 41.9 days on the lot. Not only is that 10.1% faster than September 2025, but it's almost two weeks faster on average than gas cars, which take 54.8 days to sell. Furthermore, gas car sale time increased by 19.9%. So it's getting harder to sell used gas cars, while EVs are getting easier.

Admittedly, in defense of gas cars, customers are spoiled for choice. There are far, far more gas cars available for sale—for example, Autotrader lists 1,384,383 used gas and diesel cars nationwide, but only 44,434 used EVs. There are also fewer EV models for sale, so customers aren't cross-shopping as much. Still, there's no denying that used EV demand is increasing as supply continues to grow.

There are also more options than ever in a market that was once essentially wholly dominated by Tesla. But in September, none of the top 10 fastest-selling used EV models were Teslas. There weren't any Lucids or Rivians in there, either. The quickest-selling EVs were oddly the Audi Q4 E-tron Sportback, followed by the Toyota bZX4, and Lexus RZ 300e. So it seems that used EV customers are becoming like everyone else: they just want something small and practical, with some quirky styling and a nice interior. Also on the list were the Honda Prologue, BMW iX, and even Polestar 2.

The slowest-selling EVs aren't exactly surprising, though, as they're mostly massive and expensive SUVs and trucks. The Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-seller by a huge margin, but it's also uber-expensive. It was followed by the GMC Sierra EV, Chevy Silverado EV, and the Volvo EX90. The Hummer EV was on the list, too, proving that GM's Ultium trucks aren't exactly popular on the used market.

One of the reasons why used Teslas might not have sold as quickly as other EVs is that their prices have increased. The Tesla Model S and Model X both saw used price increases of 22% and 18%, respectively. That is good for the two highest of any used car on the market, regardless of powertrain.

It's interesting to see used EVs increasing in selling speed, showing that customers are willing to go electric when the vehicle type and price suits their needs. And now that data has come out proving that EVs don't lose as much range over time as previously thought, it seems that used EVs are becoming better and better buys.

NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Nearly 50 years after leaving Earth, NASA's Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone that will highlight just how far humanity's most distant spacecraft has traveled. But keeping the aging explorer operational has become an increasingly difficult challenge as its power supply slowly fades.

NASA engineers recently achieved two important developments in their effort to extend the mission. In September, they completed a complex energy conservation project designed to preserve the spacecraft's remaining scientific capabilities. Then, on October 20, Voyager 1 unexpectedly resumed communication with Earth after a mysterious 48-hour interruption.

NASA Engineers Find a Clever Way to Save Power

In early September, the Voyager team successfully replaced three devices aboard Voyager 1 with alternatives that consume less electricity. The carefully coordinated operation, nicknamed the "Big Bang," took months to prepare and was completed approximately six weeks after engineers carried out an identical procedure on Voyager 2.

The upgrade is expected to extend the operating lives of Voyager 1's remaining scientific instruments, allowing the spacecraft to continue collecting valuable information from interstellar space longer than previously expected.

Both Voyager spacecraft generate electricity using radioisotope thermoelectric generators. These systems produce electrical power from the heat released as plutonium undergoes radioactive decay. As that process continues, the spacecraft gradually lose generating capacity, with each probe experiencing a decline of approximately 4 watts annually.

After almost five decades in space, that steady loss has left engineers with very little power to spare. To keep the missions operating, NASA has progressively shut down equipment that is no longer essential.

The Big Bang presented an especially difficult engineering challenge because all three replacements had to happen simultaneously. The six devices involved help maintain temperatures inside the spacecraft despite the extreme cold of space. Replacing the three original devices together was necessary to reduce electricity consumption while preserving the proper distribution of heat throughout Voyager 1.

Keeping Voyager 1's Science Mission Alive

Power limitations have already forced NASA to deactivate two of Voyager 1's scientific instruments in recent years. When the spacecraft launched in 1977, it carried 10 instruments dedicated to scientific research. Several were shut down after Voyager completed its encounters with the outer planets, while others remained active to investigate increasingly distant regions of space.

Among the areas studied was the outer heliosphere, the enormous region of particles and magnetic fields produced by the Sun. Both Voyager spacecraft have since crossed beyond this boundary into interstellar space, making them the only spacecraft ever to directly examine the environment outside the Sun's heliosphere.

Preserving their remaining instruments is particularly important because no other missions can currently collect measurements from this distant region. Without the Big Bang upgrade, NASA would have faced the possibility of shutting down another Voyager 1 instrument as early as summer 2027.

Mysterious Communication Loss Raises New Questions

Even with the successful power conservation effort, Voyager 1 continues to encounter unexpected problems.

NASA temporarily lost contact with the spacecraft on October 18 and 19, when the agency's Deep Space Network failed to receive its radio signal during two scheduled communication attempts separated by 24 hours.

The network consists of large radio antennas at three locations around the world, allowing NASA to exchange signals with spacecraft exploring the Moon and more distant destinations. At the time of the interruption, Voyager 1 was approximately 16 billion miles (24 billion kilometers) from Earth.

After two unsuccessful attempts to detect the spacecraft, its signal unexpectedly returned on October 20, roughly 48 hours after the interruption began. Communication has remained established since then, and engineers subsequently sent commands to investigate the problem.

NASA has not yet determined exactly what caused the incident. However, engineers discovered that one set of Voyager 1's thrusters had stopped operating and that the spacecraft had automatically activated its backup thrusters.

This behavior is part of a built-in safety system known as fault protection. When the onboard computers recognize a potential problem with active equipment, they can switch to backup hardware, place the spacecraft into a stable configuration, and suspend normal activities. This gives controllers on Earth an opportunity to investigate and determine the appropriate response.

"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," said Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "We're relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened."

Voyager 1 Approaches a Historic One-Light-Day Milestone

While NASA continues investigating the communication interruption, Voyager 1 is moving toward another remarkable achievement.

Traveling through interstellar space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), the spacecraft is expected to reach a distance of 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth on November 18. That distance equals one light-day, meaning it takes light an entire 24 hours to travel between Earth and the probe.

No other human-made object has ever reached such a distance.

The milestone also illustrates the extraordinary challenges of communicating with a spacecraft so far from home. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so commands transmitted from Earth will require a full day to reach Voyager 1. Any response sent back will take another 24 hours, creating a total communication delay of 48 hours.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL.

Crossing the one-light-day threshold will not produce any physical change in Voyager 1 or its surroundings. The spacecraft will continue traveling through the same interstellar environment, unaware that it has passed a milestone of special significance to people on Earth.

Instead, the achievement serves as a powerful reminder of the enormous distances separating objects in the universe and the remarkable endurance of a spacecraft launched nearly half a century ago. Despite fading power, aging equipment, and unexpected technical problems, Voyager 1 continues its historic journey farther from Earth than any other human-made object.

Afterwords – Marvel’s Wolverine

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

We interviewed game director Mike Daly after the launch of Insomniac’s recent Wolverine game to get his take on what makes Wolverine and Spidey different to work on, his thoughts on breadcrumb trails, and why Logan can’t ever seem to get the girl.

Insomniac had extensive experience working on well-known superhero characters before starting on Wolverine. Early on, what traits or qualities of Logan as a story character and playable avatar did you know you wanted to focus on, distinct from the Spider-Man games and character?

From a story perspective, we wanted Logan to be a man with centuries of experiences that he can’t remember, creating a mix of being worn, wizened, and cynical. His resilience makes him fearless, which comes through in his candid manner, and he can’t ignore his sense of justice, as much as he would like to.

For gameplay, it was important that players felt the difference made by his healing factor, claws, berserker rage, animalistic strength, enhanced senses, his adamantium skeleton, and corresponding weight.

In both story and gameplay, emotionally and physically, Wolverine is a hero who gets hurt and feels that pain deeply but always gets back up again and presses on. This dogged resilience was really important to us and a central theme of story and gameplay.

Wolverine is more of a linear adventure than the open-world exploration of a big city seen in Spidey. In my playthrough, that added to the sense of relentless pacing that characterizes Wolverine as a fictional lead. Was that part of the thinking behind why the game was built that way, or was the more linear path there for other reasons?

Ultimately, we made a game suited for a Wolverine story that had comic book pacing – action and meaningful story development on every page.

We experimented with different structures and stories, evaluating from the perspective of: “Is this the best way to do Wolverine justice?” As the various things we tried didn’t feel right, we had to challenge our assumptions and look to our favorite Wolverine stories for inspiration, which led us to where we ended up – a story with momentum in which every beat felt authentic to the character.

Scenes and gameplay sequences that might have been fine in other games but didn’t strongly evoke Wolverine undermined the consistency of the fantasy we were trying to create, so we tried to keep things very focused.

After the game’s release, there was an active online conversation about some of the breadcrumb-trail guidance the game offers to lead you to pickups, or to mark the continued golden path of progression. What was the thinking internally about that design decision, and your take on the debate after the game launched?

Our thinking was that it was essential to make the player feel like they were empowered by Logan’s enhanced senses, a canonical mutant ability, enabling players to do things they could not with other characters. We wanted to weave that power into as many parts of the game as we could, so that if Logan could smell or hear something relevant, the player could see it too.

For collectibles, we wanted players to enjoy seeking out and spotting senses cues, enabling you to find things that would have been obscure to other characters. Using the cues, players can cover a lot of ground without feeling the need to scour, maintaining story and action momentum.

After the game launched, we saw feedback from players that interpreted senses as abstract designer guidance, along with a desire for options in how they approached exploration and discovery. Fortunately, we have been able to incorporate this feedback from players in our post-launch patches. One aspect we’ve improved is the scent trail’s organic presentation, so they give a stronger impression that they belong in the world rather than being an abstraction. For players that want to do more manual exploration, we’ve added options to remove the sense cues for optional collectibles, and one to make scent trails dimmer until the player requests a hint.

Ultimately, enhanced senses are still essential to creating an authentic Wolverine, and that’s still reflected in the cinematic and environmental storytelling of the game. I think it’s great that on top of that, players now have more flexibility in how they experience them.

As a longtime comics fan, I found Logan’s combat system especially exciting, particularly for the relentless forward momentum it provided. What do you think were some of the keys to nailing that dynamic, as distinct from other high-quality third-person action games?

There were a few key elements we wanted to get right - Logan’s resilience, rage, claw feel, and overall lethality.

For resilience, Logan’s healing factor needed to feel important for survival - a prominent element of the system. A natural starting point there was to try continual regeneration so you could outlast enemies, but that quickly fell apart as it incentivized the player to slow the pace of combat or even retreat for maximum advantage. Even though it was incredibly effective at enabling survival, it was also hard to notice by the player so it didn’t feel prominent.

The key to solving this problem was making a connection between rage and healing factor. The Last Stand mechanic is a healing surge that can happen when you lose all your health, themed as using adrenaline to keep Logan’s heart beating. This incentivized aggression and made a space for an up-close look at visceral healing.

Speaking of rage, it’s the backbone of the combat system where being an indicator of momentum is key. At the low end of rage, you don’t have the safety net of Last Stand, so your decision-making naturally biases towards survival; ensuring you prioritize threat assessment and defense. As you climb into the middle tier, you have the leeway to push your luck for longer combos or barrages that let you build up rage and get kills faster. Finally, you get to rage tier 3, where the quick decay of rage makes your rate of kills the top priority, so you might prefer to attack groups over ranged stragglers just for the improved kill density. Beyond the mechanics, we change the presentation of combat, especially through Logan’s animations and exertion to reflect his state of mind. The presentation and systemic incentives drive the player into a frenzy, just like Wolverine.

We invested a lot in the details of claw feel to make sure it was distinct from general game attacks. Claws shred, so we added locational body damage to our enemies to reflect that, along with a dynamic blood system where it globs together as it is spilled, splatters on contact with characters or the environment, drips down the walls, diffuses in the water, and other details. Many kills throughout combat are punctuated with custom animations with cinematic camera work that pushes in and frames the puncturing of claws into the body for a strong impression of the connection and weight of the puncture. Severing limbs on these attacks is an occasional reminder of how sharp Logan’s adamantium claws are. Reinforcing this is top-notch sound and haptics design, so each hit registers.

The last aspect I’ll touch on is lethality, the rate at which Wolverine is able to dispatch enemies and vice versa. We found that fights where enemies were more technical and could survive a lot undermined what players expected to experience as Wolverine, which was aggressively and lethally tearing through a lot of enemies. On the other hand, combat was less exciting if the enemies didn’t feel like a serious and deadly threat, and you didn’t feel like Wolverine if a little bit of caution could enable you to defend perfectly and avoid all damage.

These aspects led us towards encounters where you confronted large groups of enemies that were highly aggressive, to the point of feeling unfair. Enemies can’t believably go toe-to-toe with Wolverine alone, even world-class mercenaries, so their strategy is in group coordination, which creates a counterweight to Wolverine’s own rage-based momentum.

Marvel’s Wolverine draws in a number of characters from across the X-Men comic mythology, but notably makes no mention of some foundational figures of that fiction – Professor Xavier and Magneto. That, in turn, leads to dramatically different lives for characters like Jean Grey or Logan. Is the narrative you crafted an intentional exploration of a world where those figures weren’t present in the early days of mutant emergence?

I would say it was more of an exploration of the character than the world. We wanted a story where Logan is pulled into conflict not because he’s a crusader, but because there’s no other option. There are no X-Men to help. His growth as a person should be a challenging journey, which could go unearned if he was surrounded by wise, supportive, heroic characters pushing him in the right direction. In contrast, his dynamic with the members of Team X evokes his struggle. The adversity to personal growth is what makes it interesting.

Jean does end up being the person that pushes him in the right direction, and that works because they can relate to each other, having had similar struggles.

In several versions of Marvel storytelling, Jean and Logan share a special bond, but Jean ultimately chooses Scott Summers as a partner. But even without that barrier in your story, Logan still hits some roadblocks to love. Is Wolverine fundamentally a better character when he just can’t get the girl?

The way I would put it is that a Wolverine story is fundamentally better when you empathize with Logan’s pain and admire him for pressing on despite it. That goes for his emotional pain as much as physical. He’s a tragic character in this regard – all he wants is to be at peace but can never find it for long.

Wolverine gets to take on a lot of the “heavy hitters” of his comic mythology in different boss fights throughout the game. When you began development, do you recall who the very first character was that you decided he simply had to fight in your game?

Sabretooth. No character is a better foil for Logan. His inner turmoil and chaotic behavior helps illustrate Logan’s own inner beast and his struggle to resist it. Sabretooth’s strength and mutant powers also provide a mirror to Logan in combat, and his savagery creates shocking moments that leave an impression. We knew an epic confrontation with Sabretooth was going to be a thing from the start.

Holiday Gift Guide 2026

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

With the holiday gift-giving season upon us, it’s time to think about the gaming fans in your life and find the ideal present to brighten their day. And if you’re the gamer in the family, we always encourage you to circle relevant items in the coming pages and leave your magazine open in hard-to-miss locations around the house. We’ve scoured dozens of tech products, tabletop games, collectibles, and more to select and highlight some of the coolest items we found this year.

We recommended the Board shortly after its launch, but with its expanded game library and lower price than first-adopter rates, this holiday season is an ideal time to make the leap. This family-friendly platform features original games that sit comfortably between the digital and physical divide. The horizontally placed screen shows the backdrop of one of the several included games, or the sold-separately add-on games that have popped in since launch. Each game has its own real physical play pieces that interact with the action onscreen, often in innovative and charming ways. Think of it as the best of both worlds between board games and video games, and you’ll get what they’re shooting for here. $399

Few additions to the latest Dungeons & Dragons rules pack as much punch and value as this new expansion, focusing on ways to develop further and evolve the use of magic across your tabletop gaming sessions. New subclasses, spells, creatures, magical items, and factions add thoughtful, intriguing options for both players looking to play someone new and DMs hunting for new story hooks and challenges. $50

If you’re as excited as we are about this month’s celebration of the Tomb Raider legacy (see p. 40), this centerpiece statue is an ideal fit for your collection. Standing roughly nine inches in height, Lara is poised for exploration in her original classic garb. The sculpt strikes a perfect balance between crisp detail and stylistic presentation, in line with that early version of the character; the metallic blue motorcycle paint is especially striking. $250

For players longing for the glory days of stand-up arcade games, it’s hard to beat Arcade 1Up’s approach. The team’s sturdy cabinets look and sound great as a marquee feature of your game room. The new Outrun machine features much of the original display art, a bright 19-inch screen, and responsive gas and brake pedals as you steer around those tight corners. Sega has packed in OutRun, Turbo OutRun, OutRunners, and Power Drift. If old-school racing isn’t your thing, look for cabinets that run the gamut from Pac-Man to Joust to Claw Machines. $629.99

The long-running Nendoroid figures continue to be an attractive but still affordable choice for building collections across numerous fan-favorite series. There are somewhere around 2000 characters at this point! New entries like the Genshin Impact collection make a strong case for the line. The look is chibi, the quality is excellent, poseability is high, and customizable face and accessory parts let you change up your display over time. $46

We’ve previously sung the praises of Libernovo’s versatile approach to an ergonomic gaming chair, which includes a lumbar stretch functionality, a steady recline option for comfortable pushback without sudden shifts, and dynamically adjusting parts as you move through your day. The Maxis line does all that, but addresses one of the fundamental problems for at least some users with the original – it wasn’t big enough. With features like a wider base and longer headrest reach, the Maxis aims to provide the same comfort to the players who are tall or wide enough to need the extra breathing room. $1119

Privacy around smart glasses has been a major point of contention as wearable tech continues to expand. Even G2s have a clear answer to that issue by consciously leaving out a camera. Instead, these glasses focus on productivity and specific tasks, like real-time translation into 35 languages, in-lens teleprompters for presentations, and calendar notifications – all presented in a readable display that is largely invisible from the outside. $600

If you’re the player on your team who likes to have easy access to soundboards and real-time voice changing, the Key Pocket could be just the ticket. This small device straps onto your phone for mobile play, but it’s also compatible with consoles, Discord, Twitch, or just about any place you want to tweak audio on the fly. A free tier gives you access to some voice-changing and sounds, while a separate subscription opens up hundreds of thousands of additional options. But be warned: we can’t help you after your friends abandon you for that baby voice you won’t stop using. $99

The question of the best bang for your buck in modern consoles has become extraordinarily complicated, especially as tech prices have soared in recent years. There’s no right answer, but Sony’s high-end machine walks the line of offering extremely high-tier performance without escalating to even higher-priced gaming PCs. Higher and more consistent frame rates than on standard PS5, advanced ray tracing, and an increasing number of games that feature enhanced PSSR image options all add up to a better gaming experience, if you’re ready to make the significant price jump. $900

If the gamer in your life is looking for a stylish, understated way to express their love of the hobby, Anicorn’s designer watch collaboration with PlayStation could be a standout option. Available in black and a slick silver/white combo, the minimalist timepiece includes the familiar face buttons of Sony’s controller encased in an oil-injection display so they slowly and freely float across the watch as you move. $250

It’s a safe bet you’ve at least seen the popular Shashibo puzzle cubes by this point. We’ve been fans of their brain-teasing, fidgety fun for some time. Battle Shapes takes the core concept – reshaping the box into various distinct magnetically-locked shapes – and extends it into a timed game experience, playable solo or head-to-head. By targeting specific shapes, you significantly improve your speed with the toy, and scannable QR codes on the cards offer clear tutorials for each shape so you can prep for competition. $50

While the vast majority of gamers looking for good personal audio are going to be okay with a larger set of cans over their ears, We know more than a few players for whom that’s a definite no – for comfort, awareness of surrounding sounds, or other reasons. The Arc 5 earbuds aim to solve for that, with an over-ear design that feels extremely comfortable. And because they sit on the ear, you can still hear what’s going on around you. While that limits some aspects of the final sound quality, the inclusion of THX certification, Dolby Atmos optimization, and Dynamic Bass Enhancement helps to ensure audio is still very strong. $230

Across Lego’s many recent themes, Tolkien’s legendarium has offered some stellar sets. The largest yet is the capital of Gondor, with an astonishing 8,278 pieces and a height of roughly two feet. The castle/city build is impressive, featuring tons of interesting angles and turns. The finished product aims to offer the best of both worlds in presentation – a microscale representation of the front façade and a reverse minifigure-scale Hall of Kings. We especially like the inclusion of Denethor’s cherry tomatoes. $650

The original Azul is often cited as a foundational entry in modern board gaming. The “Kids” versions of celebrated titles aren’t always a sure bet, but this one holds up to scrutiny. Azul Kids lowers the complexity threshold but keeps the foundational strategic thinking. Players lay out uniquely shaped tiles into mosaic frameworks in colorful, appealing patterns; the basic concept of the original inspiration is clear, and kids as young as five can grasp and enjoy the fun. $25

Many corners of the collecting world have embraced the fun (and frequent despair) of blind boxes, where you never know exactly who you’ll get in a given series. Funism has a strong track record for quality, offering adorable smaller figures like their latest line of Evangelion collectibles. Each figure stands nearly four inches and features both human characters and mecha. You can buy singles and roll the dice, or purchase larger sets with a no-duplicates guarantee, which can save a lot of heartache if you’re trying to line your whole shelf. $21

If you’re going to spring for a high-end keyboard for PC gaming, it’s important that you like the feel of the keys. The slightly smaller overall 75% size profile of this Blackwidow has no impact on the great feel of typing – a clear highlight for the unit. The customizable, colored backlights are also a big selling point, as is the side command dial and built-in OLED display, which can be tweaked to show PC performance, GIFs, lighting brightness, and more. It’s a strong contender in a crowded field, and justifies its price with both comfort and customizability. $300

Beautiful, vibrant art and a refreshing take on the classic area-control board game genre are the two strongest reasons to take a close look at Wroth. Players control one of five races vying for supremacy across a conflict-ridden peninsula. Factions are asymmetric, so everyone has unique capabilities, and that adds significant replayability. Players roll and draft dice, allowing distinct actions that move the game forward. And move it does; unlike many games of this ilk, Wroth can be learned quickly and played to completion in a little over an hour. $65

Console and computer hardware prices are skyrocketing with no sign of slowing, and perhaps as a result, retro gaming handhelds are gaining popularity. Many quality devices are available, but what sets the Evercade Nexus apart is its officially licensed game cartridges. Imagine the nostalgic joy of a Game Boy, but with a cartridge that includes both Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie. The cartridge boxes even include manuals. For fans of physical media, Evercade Nexus is a great option. $199

This tiny USB-C plug-in (with included USB-A adapter) solves a bunch of audio challenges in one uniform device. It offers high-resolution Bluetooth transmission on iPhone, high-bitrate audio transmission to compatible LDAC headphones, enables high-quality Bluetooth output from your PC, and even low-latency Bluetooth audio on PS5 and Switch. In short, it takes a huge number of products with a USB port and ensures a dynamic Bluetooth audio connection with relative ease. $99

The original MV6 is a familiar sight on streams thanks to its clear voice reproduction and overall ease of use. Shure has built on that success with the Gen 2, offering an excellent standalone mic that doesn’t break the bank. Available in black or white, the Gen 2 features a handy auto-level mode that keeps volume even as you adjust your own amplitude, an adjustable denoiser for your space, a longer cable for out-of-the-box convenience, and three presets for plug-and-play use. In short, it’s an excellent choice if you want great performance without needing an audio engineering degree. $169

XR Glasses are still fighting for awareness, but once you try them, it’s easy to see why the concept is on the rise. Viture’s Pro 2 makes an impressive case for adoption, with a competitive price point, comfortable wear, and a giant 146-inch screen that floats in front of your face for gaming or work on your PC or phone. The display is crisp, bright, and impressive, even as the glasses are light and easy to use. With a mobile dock mini (sold separately), you can even snap onto a Switch 2 with ease and start playing instantly. $299

Role-playing gamers have several excellent universal systems to pick between when considering a story or campaign idea that might fall outside traditional genre staples. Among many good options, Cypher stands out as one of the very best. The system uses a rules-light, narrative-focused approach that prioritizes player-driven storytelling across everything from hard sci-fi to superheroes to intrigue- driven espionage. This is the corebook that’s needed to run and play the full system; additional books only add options. $50

As gamers have continually migrated toward personal audio that can rock amazing sound without disturbing the whole house, high-end premium headphones have become a dangerously competitive space. Turtle Beach meets that challenge head-on, with a robust option that sounds beautiful in use. The Stealth Pro II boasts the slick ability to wirelessly switch between different devices, which is awesome if you’re one of those players who regularly jumps between platforms to play your favorite titles. Like the whole category, it’s a lot to spend on a headset, but Dolby Atmos, active noise cancellation, and 60mm dual drivers all add up to a powerful argument. $300

With an increasing number of top-tier console and PC games like Resident Evil Village, No Man’s Sky, and Dead Cells now available on iOS, not to mention the consistent quality of Apple Arcade, Apple phones remain the best mobile platform for gaming. The 18 Pro Max phone has implemented a number of tweaks that strengthen the platform, including higher memory, much faster graphics processing, impressive HDR performance, and notably improved battery life, all adding up to a gaming experience that is working hard to justify your playtime when away from home. Starting at $1299

SteelSeries is best known for its strong audio line-up, but its push into premium-tier controllers exhibits a similar flair for quality and usability. The new Aeon Pro has a lot to recommend it as your go-to Xbox, PC, or mobile choice. The two included batteries (one of which can always be charging in the dock) ensure essentially unlimited playtime. The full-pull or hair triggers and buttons are clicky and satisfying, and the Hall Effect thumbsticks are built to minimize any drift. Textured handgrips and overall heft are ideal. And an onboard OLED lets you adjust profiles and button assignments, switch between platforms, and check battery at a glance. $260

Valve’s pricey VR headset isn’t a revolution in the medium, but the company has been invested in the technology since its inception. As a result, the Steam Frame is a very good, very comfortable headset. Like its competition, the Quest, its best use is playing games locally on the headset, and Steam’s library is vast and interesting. Wireless connected play to a powerful PC is also well done, but currently the included Wireless Adapter is not fully compatible with the Steam Machine – a baffling limitation we were shocked to confirm. VR is an expensive sub-hobby within video games, but Steam Frame is among the best ways to explore and enjoy it. $1059

Many of the coolest “gaming lights” focus on the flexibility and fun of bright RGB customization. While we’re fans of that aesthetic, it leaves others out in the cold who might want something a bit more natural. The Elements hex panels feature a natural wood-inspired panel, customizable “scenes” like a campfire glow, and can react to both music and touch, with adjustable ambient white light to keep the vibe relaxed. $200

Kyle Hilliard contributed to this article.

Cover Reveal – Tomb Raider: Legacy Of Atlantis

Game Informer’s next cover story is Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, the upcoming reimagining of the original 1996 Tomb Raider arriving on February 12. Since that game celebrates the franchise’s 30th anniversary this year, we’re doing the same with a double-whammy of Tomb Raider features.

We visited Crystal Dynamics’ office to play Legacy of Atlantis for several hours, including an exclusive tour of the Greece section. For our 12-page cover story, we spoke to key team members at Crystal Dynamics and Flying Wild Hog to learn why it’s tackling Lara Croft’s seminal adventure once again (having already remade the game once in Tomb Raider: Anniversary), how this version of the game differs from previous incarnations and why, discuss the teams' controversial use of AI development tools, and how Legacy of Atlantis plants seeds for the upcoming Tomb Raider: Catalyst.

The issue also includes a six-page retrospective of Tomb Raider’s 30-year history, with insights from Crystal Dynamics. This celebration is reflected in our cover art, designed by Tomb Raider franchise art director Brenoch Adams, which showcases every version of Lara Croft from the Core Design, Legend, Survivor, and current eras.

The December issue also marks the return of our annual (and very large) holiday buyers guide, featuring curated gift suggestions for the gamers in your life ahead of the winter holidays. Furthermore, we’ve created a list of family-friendly games to enjoy with younger relatives during upcoming holiday gatherings. Guest contributor Veerender Singh Jubbal writes about India's emerging game development scene and how its community is helping elevate local titles to an international stage. Ahead of the launch of Ryu Ga Gatoku’s Stranger Than Heaven, executive editor Brian Shea played a new section of the era-spanning Yakuza/Like a Dragon prequel while picking the brains of its lead designers for details on the game’s plot, themes, and time periods. Senior associate editor Wesley LeBlanc shares his glowing impressions of Murals, the colorful, fairy-tale-inspired adventure from Disney Illusion Island developer Dlala Studios, whom he spoke with about the game’s conception.

We also have plenty of previews for upcoming games including Final Fantasy VII Revelation, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, Muramasa: Revenant Blades, Fate/Extra Record, Tiny Metal 2, Mr. Records, and Eternal Anima. We also have reviews for Gears of War: E-Day, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Control Resonant, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Silent Hill: Downfall, and many more.
