Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

WoW: Forever Is Giving Players A Big Damage Boost For Launch

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

World of Warcraft: Forever is changing in some major ways for launch, with Blizzard revealing classes across the board will deal more damage as it pursues design solutions that better fit in with Forever's combat.

In a lengthy developer note attached to Forever's launch patch notes, Blizzard outlined its philosophy for its latest version of WoW. It said during the game's nearly month-long beta that it was trying to keep player power in check. That meant every time it gave a class new tools and abilities, it had to tone down others to compensate. Blizzard now thinks that was the wrong approach.

"Those reductions left some iconic abilities feeling lackluster, and closed the door to other potentially exciting design options," Blizzard said. "So over the last two weeks, we've raised damage on classes across the game, and have increased the health of higher-level creatures to compensate."

In addition to classes simply doing more damage, classes themselves are changing in major ways. Elemental Shamans, for example, have had Lava Burst, a key part of their class during the beta, removed entirely. It's an example of what Blizzard said was the developer hastily "turning to Burning Crusade or Wrath-era solutions" rather than creating new ideas for how classes should play in Forever compared to previous versions of WoW.

"Our aim in class design is not perfect numerical equality, but rather for every class to feel valuable to groups they join, with powerful, unforgettable moments brought on by mastering them," Blizzard said. "In Forever this is accomplished by doubling down on the strengths and differences that make each class unique, rather than overly unifying them."

Alongside Shaman, a number of other classes have received significant changes going into launch, particularly Paladin and Rogue, with much of their talent trees almost completely reworked. Every class has received some balance changes.

Though the patch notes are largely dedicated to class changes, there are some other adjustments coming for launch as well. There are a number of tweaks to the game's controller support and bug fixes for various quests. Blizzard stated it additionally increased enemy respawn rates in the world for launch, particularly in lower-level zones. Its goal isn't to completely remove contention for spawns but to make it so players aren't hitting hard bottlenecks.

"Once the initial launch surge of low-level characters has settled down, we will adjust the lower-level zones down to more typical rates," Blizzard said. 

You can find the full WoW: Forever launch patch notes below. WoW: Forever launches November 4. Ahead of launch, read up on the best WoW: Forever addons to install so you're ready on day one. In other news, Blizzard revealed its plans for how often players should expect Forever updates, as well how it's looking to avoid dead servers in the future.

WoW: Forever November 2 Launch Patch Notes

Bug Fixes

  • Throw will now correctly use the 0.5 second windup timer (was incorrectly using the throwing weapon’s attack speed).
  • Legacy Reward - Replica Ironforge Air Rifle can now correctly be used on allies that also have one equipped.
    • Duration of the quitter debuff reduced to 40 seconds (was 5 minutes).
    • Duration of the stun reduced to 2.5 seconds (was 3 seconds).
  • All Races now have the correct amount of base stats. For example, Tauren Warriors now start with the correct +5 strength relative to Human Warriors (was incorrectly +2). This fix was also applied to High Order and Windshaper Skyborne base stats.
  • Roots that occur from Procs now correctly have Diminishing Returns. Includes Frostbite, Entrapment, Improved Wing Clip, Counterattack, and Improved Hamstring.

Classes

  • Developer’s notes: Over the course of Beta, we came to the realization that trying to hold ourselves roughly to Classic power budgets for each class meant that every new element we added needed to come at the expense of something else. Those reductions left some iconic abilities feeling lackluster, and closed the door to other potentially exciting design options. So over the last two weeks, we’ve raised damage on classes across the game, and have increased the health of higher level creatures to compensate. This additional “headroom” has allowed us to tune things to a place that we hope feels better overall. Beyond that, some of this round of changes reflects areas where we were likely hasty in turning to Burning Crusade- or Wrath-era solutions rather than carving out new ones that better fit into the Forever combat model. Our aim in class design is not perfect numerical equality, but rather for every class to feel valuable to the groups they join, with powerful, unforgettable moments brought on by mastering them. In Forever this is accomplished by doubling down on the strengths and differences that make each class unique, rather than overly unifying them.
  • Developers’ notes: We’ve used the data and feedback gathered during Beta testing to get everything tuned to a reasonable place. However, the only true test of that tuning is the game itself. With the exception of bugs and serious outliers, we don’t plan on making big tuning changes between now and the opening of the raids next month. Once we have sufficient data from players leveling past 30 and engaging in a wide range of content, we expect that we will do a large tuning pass based on our data. And this is all merely a starting point for the classes in Forever, which will continue to evolve over the course of the months and years ahead just as they did following the original launch in 2004.
  • Various talents no longer have a penalty to their chance to trigger when casting spells of a low rank.
    • This penalty does still apply to Blizzard. Blizzard continues to have a reduced chance to trigger Arcane Concentration, Frostbite, and Fingers of Frost when casting a rank learned more than 12 levels lower than the caster’s current level.
  • Learning new spells will no longer cause them to be automatically added to your action bars.
  • Training costs on have been adjusted for all classes.
    • Most abilities learned at the same level have the same cost to train, with the exception of Priest race-specific abilities.
    • Total cost to train class abilities from 1-60 is now between 206 and 207 gold for all classes.
    • Warlocks costs are reduced by the expected costs of buying Grimoires for their pets.

      • Improved Keyring navigation and highlighting.

WoW: Forever Shamans Are Protesting Class Changes After Being “Completely Ignored”

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

World of Warcraft: Forever just received a massive batch of class-balance updates ahead of launch that have boosted power across the board, but one group of players isn't happy with the changes: Shamans.

Developer Blizzard recently released Forever's launch patch notes based on feedback and data accumulated during the beta, resulting in a power spike for all classes and major reworks for classes like Paladin and Rogue. Shamans, too, received some significant changes, most notably the removal of a key Elemental specialization ability, Lava Burst, along with any interactions other abilities had with it.

It's that change, and other changes to specialization-specific abilities like Restoration's Riptide and Enhancement's Maelstrom Weapon, that have resulted in the WoW Classic Shaman Discord going into lockdown in protest. The entire server, which has around 80,000 members, has been made read-only, with a message declaring the reason for why it took what it described as such a "drastic measure."

"Community feedback gets completely ignored and class fantasies are getting destroyed," the server declared. "With this we intend to give them [Blizzard] a sign and show them that the community is not [happy] with how they approached our beloved class. Give us back our class and spec identities and fantasies."

While the protest is in regards to class changes in Forever specifically, the server is also home to Shaman discussions as they relate to other "classic" versions of the game as well, including WoW Classic and Mists of Pandaria Classic. As of writing, all of those channels are also locked and set to read-only. 

In a follow-up post, the server went into more detail about its complaints in regards to how Blizzard has approached Forever's Shaman design. It stated its complaints aren't about "damage output." It also made clear the server will re-open "regardless of the outcome," but that it felt like its feedback through "legitimate" channels were being ignored. 

The server then proceeded to list what it viewed as wrong with various ability changes for each Shaman specialization. It additionally called attention to what it called the "hybrid spell power issue," where spell power and intellect gear seems to be better for not only Elemental but also Enhancement, muddying the identity between the two specializations. 

Blizzard has previously said it doesn't want "hybrid" classes that can deal damage and heal, like Shamans, to deal more damage than dedicated DPS classes. Players in the WoW community refer to this idea as the "hybrid tax," something those running the Shaman Discord said they are fine with if it means Shaman class design is improved.

"Truthfully, hybrid tax us all you want if the result is a cohesive class with strong class fantasy elements that are actually represented in our playstyles," it said. 

This isn't the first time a WoW class Discord shut down in protest of how class changes. As pointed out by Wowhead, back in August 2025, the modern WoW Paladin Discord was partially closed in protest of the Retribution specialization's raid performance. In that case, only Retribution-specific channels were locked, and the entire protest lasted less than 24 hours. Blizzard did announce Retribution Paladin buffs shortly after, though it's unclear if those changes came at least in part due to the server protest or not.

How long the WoW Classic Shaman Discord remains in lockdown remains to be seen, but Forever launches November 4. Blizzard recently said it doesn't expect to make any more major class changes for at least another month.

Given that Sony holds the marketing rights for Grand Theft Auto 6, Microsoft has had to get creative to promote the open-world crime game for Xbox--and the company's latest effort in that department goes big.

Say Hello to the X-Bite, a playable Xbox Series X console that was designed to look like it was swallowed whole by one of Florida's millions of alligators. Microsoft only made one of these ornate consoles, and you have to win a contest to get it.

Microsoft's blog post doesn't mention GTA 6 or Rockstar Games, but Xbox marketing boss Josh Munsee said the system has "pure Miami vibes," and that's a pretty obvious reference to GTA 6 given the game takes place in a stand-in, Vice City, for the popular Florida city. The blog post says the winner of the console can play "some of the biggest games of the year" using it, and that's no doubt another nod to GTA 6.

"This November, Xbox is heading to Florida--home to incredible wildlife, unforgettable places, and every now and then, stories you have to see to believe," Microsoft said in its announcement of the X-Bite.

The X-Bite is about five feet long, and the console itself sits inside the alligator, with the Nexus/Guide button illuminated through the gator's skin. The lucky winner will also get a custom Xbox controller with simulated bite marks on it.

The custom console was designed by creature animatronic specialist John Nolan Studio, which did work for The Witcher and Jurassic World Dominion.

Microsoft's fine print states that the gator console is a "custom fabrication" and wasn't made from a real alligator. "No actual alligators were used or harmed in the making of this console," Microsoft said. The estimated value of the console is $800, Microsoft said.

You can enter for a chance to win the X-Bite by following Xbox on X, Instagram, or TikTok, reposting the sweepstakes post, and then add #XbiteSweepstakes to your repost. You'll also need to have a public account.

The sweepstakes runs now through November 10. The winner, who will be chosen by a random draw, will have 48 hours to respond if they're selected. "Miss the window, and this gator makes a clean getaway," Microsoft said in yet another reference to GTA 6.

GTA 6 is getting special treatment for its PS5 edition, and this has so far included a limited-edition DualSense controller inspired by the game and trailers for GTA 6 that end by telling people the game "plays best" on PS5. The game's recent launch trailer does not include the Xbox logo, either.

GTA 6 is of course not exclusive to Xbox, and there is no evidence that it "plays best" on PS5.

According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 has sold about 2 million copies so far on Xbox Series X|S, compared to 5.75 million on PS5. Xbox is not worried the PS5 version massively pacing ahead of Xbox, in part because the 74%/26% split in favor of PS5 over Xbox reflects Xbox's current share of the console market. GTA 6 is breaking records already for Xbox, the company has said.

Microsoft takes a 30% cut of games sold on the Xbox platform, so that could end up being a huge number when the game launches, even if it's far behind PS5. At about 2 million copies sold on Xbox so far, according to Sensor Tower, that's $192 million in gross revenue; Xbox's cut would be about $57.6 million. Sensor Tower has said the majority of GTA 6 preorders should come in the final week before release, and could reach 25 million.

If the split stays about where it is now, that would be about 6.5 million units on Xbox by launch, generating more than $170 million in platform fees paid to Xbox. Of course, these are just ballpark estimates, but it's a sure thing that GTA 6 is going to be a big deal for Xbox. Microsoft already alluded to this, as the company forecast major growth for Xbox content and services in the current quarter, and while management didn't attribute this to any particular title, the gargantuan release of GTA 6 is no doubt factored in.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

The lost malloc()

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

(Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :)

Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources. This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities.

This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation.

In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago. C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4.

Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time.

While cleaning a storage room, our staff found this tape containing UNIX v4 from Bell Labs, circa 1973

The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code.

In /usr/c/c20.c:814, from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see:

Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not.

The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk(), when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated.

And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program.

This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title.

In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c. And you see two functions there:

Seems familiar? Yep, it's mfree() with an m. These functions obviously deal with memory (de)allocation, and are the precursor to the ones we're familiar with today. But, the interfaces are different.

malloc() receives an additional first argument called mp (for "map"), and so does mfree(). What is that? Well, let's see how they're used:

So, they pass in some objects coremap and swapmap. What are those? From /usr/sys/systm.h:2:

They're just flat memory regions! So these malloc() and mfree() work on explicit memory regions! Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should. Those are just infinitely-times better interfaces than traditional malloc()/free().

Imagine using a library that has such an interface. You could deallocate all its memory resources by just discarding the entire region you delegated to it. Heap corruption bugs would be less severe because you could partition memory. You could trivially limit the amount of memory third party code allocates. The list goes on and on...

(Side note: They slightly messed up here and the regions should've been sized CMAPSIZ/2 and SMAPSIZ/2 respectively. They did fix that later.)

However, I don't think all these benefits were in the minds of Dennis and Ken. So why did they go with that interface and why did they partition memory to "core" and "swap"? The reason is, I believe, just hardware constraints. These interfaces stay like that up to V6 (maybe V7 too?), released the spring of '75, and thankfully there's an infamously good resource about that edition.

From A Commentary on the Sixth Edition UNIX Operating System by John Lions:

These are concerned with the allocation and subsequent release of two kinds of memory resources, namely:

For each of these two kinds of resource, a list of available areas is maintained within a resource "map" (either "coremap" or "swapmap"). A pointer to the appropriate resource "map" is always passed to "malloc" and "mfree" so that the routines themselves do not have to know the kind of resource with which they are dealing.

And it goes on to explain how the underlying allocation algorithm works. These do not do linear allocation (hence the mfree()). Basically, it's a list of blocks (struct map), ordered by address, where you do first-fit and also coalesce neighbour blocks.

The sixth edition is also the first where the term "arena" appears, in /usr/source/s4/alloc.s:17:

... to the topic of linear allocation... In V6's /usr/source/s1/diff1.c:88, I think the first ever version of diff(1), you find:

This is not all that much different from the previous alloc(), but this time it handles any allocation size. It uses a while to continue extending the region and stops when enough space has been reserved. The actual interesting part happens later, at unsort():143:

I'm not exactly sure what that function does, but it doesn't matter. What matters is that they allocate some memory (a = alloc(...);), then roll back the region (area = a;)! Though they subsequently just copy it to b, so it seems like this was redundant.

Most of the code directly calls malloc()/alloc() and friends, and inlines the size computation logic. Like the line we saw earlier:

I don't do that anymore, and neither should you! I use a couple macros akin to C++'s new that handle all the sizeof business. But I am a dumb-dumb. Surely these guys must've come across the same pain points, and, if so, what did they do? Let's jump to V7, released January '79, four years after V6. You find this macro:

Nice! It's interesting to note where you find it; In /usr/src/cmd/f77/defines:38 and /usr/src/cmd/make/defs:38. Slightly suspicious. The former is part of the Fortran 77 compiler and latter of make. Stuart Feldman is the person who worked on both of those programs! It's clear that multiple people were working on the system at that time. A macro like that isn't used in any other program, sadly.

V7 is the first edition where you also find the assert() macro, and it was used extensively back then too. Good job! They also significantly expanded the number of man pages. Fun fact: I did $ man V7/usr/man/man3/foo.3 -- on 47 year old pages -- and it worked first try absolutely fine.

Let's go to V8, released in February '85, four years before the first C standard. You find this wild macro in /usr/src/cmd/ideal/memut.c:7:

If someone is too harsh because you used macros, point them at the above. Usage is bit different this time:

I decided to include it because the macro zero-initialises by default whatever was allocated! You also see a more familiar-looking malloc() being used. It appears this is the edition that they switched to the more traditional malloc()/free() interfaces we know. I'll hypothesize why that is at the very end.

But it gets even more interesting. In V8 you also find these macros:

When I saw these definitions I jumped out of my chair. It's basically how I'd define it too! You'll find them in:

Unfortunately, I can't find the author(s) of any of these.

In V8, you'll also find Cfront, a.k.a. medieval C++. It's then reasonable to assume that Stroustrup was inspired by the above macros and decided to incorporate new as a language-level feature. However, in A History of C++: 1979−1991, he writes:

In Simula, it is not possible to have local or global variables of class types; that is, every object of a class must be allocated on the free store using the new operator.

Huh. So C++'s new was inspired by the programming language "Simula". It's fair to say that the macros above were likely also derived from there. But Simula was quite old even by the 70s, let alone 1985. Perhaps Stroustrup persuaded people, or wrote those macros himself. He later writes:

The new operator that both allocates memory from the free store and invokes a constructor to ensure initialization was borrowed from Simula. The delete operator was a necessary complement because I did not want C with Classes to depend on a garbage collector. The argument for the new operator can be summarized like this. Would you rather write:

and which version are you most likely to make a mistake in? The arguments against -- which were voiced quite a lot at the time -- were "but we don’t really need it," and "but someone will have used new as an identifier." Both observations are correct, of course. Introducing operator new thus made the use of free store more convenient and less error−prone. This increased its use even further so that the C free store allocation routine malloc() used to implement new became the most common performance bottleneck in real systems. [...] Having real programs spend 50% or more of their time in malloc() wasn’t acceptable.

He makes a compelling argument, which I agree with, but doesn't mention the new() macros that basically did the same thing. Although you'll find many programs in V8 that do the latter, verbose thing. Now I want to know the author(s) of those macros even more!

This is a big parentheses because I wanted to know how Simula came up with new. Wikipedia states:

Simula 67 introduced objects, classes, inheritance and subclasses, virtual procedures, coroutines, and discrete event simulation, and featured garbage collection.

And it appeared in 1967. Wow! In the 1964 report of SIMULA I, you'll find:

[...] The symbol "new" only serves to resolve an ambiguity of the identifier A inside the activity blah blah blah [...]. Elsewhere the symbol new is redundant, but can often be used to advantage to improve readability.

So it was only used to resolve grammar ambiguities (I think?). And Stroustrup re-purposed it. Clever!

The History of Simula, by Jan Rune Holmevik. Reads like (bad) Sci-Fi. All the politics nonsense aside, what I found most curious is that they completely specified the language before attempting to write a compiler for it. They started writing the first compiler atleast a year after. This would sound insane today, but I guess the cost of writing code was substantially higher back then.

Also: The development of the SIMULA languages, by the authors. I didn't read that one, although I should...

It's honestly amazing how influential Simula was. In "10.5 Operating Instruction" they even use the term "run time system" and give it the same meaning we're accustomed to.

Simula, in turn, was partly inspired by SIMSCRIPT (don't laugh). If you skim its 1962 report, you won't find a mention of new. You'll however find CREATE:

When a new Entity is created by a CREATE statement, space for storing its Attribute values is allocated in the amount specified on the Definition Form. This record is given an identification number, and the Variable specified in the CREATE statement is automatically set equal to this number.

For example, the statement "CREATE DOG CALLED FIDO" allocates the required amount of storage for the Attributes of a DOG, and sets FIDO equal to the identification number of the Attribute record.

Fascinating. The whole SIMSCRIPT report is fascinating actually, and I only briefly skimmed through it. At the beginning, it even describes something like a primitive ECS, by my understanding. At the end though it slaps you back to reality:

In V9's /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:14, part of the Sam editor by Rob Pike, you find a "generalised" version of new():

Although, by and large, almost every program doesn't do this. Most just directly call malloc() and friends, and do size calculations \w error checking at every call site. I don't know why, considering how much error-prone that is, but maybe due to inertia. It's a similar story in V10, but I didn't check it as thoroughly since it's quite big (it includes medieval GCC!).

They were so close to arenas; with linear allocation and explicit memory regions, rolling back, and even having a nice new() macro. All this is speculation at this point, but maybe some of it is correct. First of all, most programs had trivial object lifetimes. Allocate memory, read some data, process/crunch and spit out some result. You don't need any disciplined memory allocation strategy for that. You can even use malloc() for everything and let the OS reclaim it once the process exits. Given how simple malloc() was at first, it wouldn't be much of a bottleneck either. The philosophy of programs only "doing a single thing well" also fitted this pattern.

Secondly, it's clear some decisions were motivated by the very little memory they had to play with. And there was no virtual memory either (initially, that is). Nowadays, you can "allocate" however big of a memory region you want and all will probably be okay. They couldn't really do that, so they were fighting to reclaim every empty block and gap there was and scale a program's space with how much is actually needed. There's a counterpoint to this, however, because some code is confused. Sometimes you see fixed-size buffers/arrays pop up, seemingly out of nowhere, and the program bail out if they fill. I'm not sure why, but perhaps they didn't deem it worthwhile the complexity to use malloc() in those cases and/or "don't fix it if it ain't broke" kind-of thing.

And clearly, when they could get away with simple linear allocation, they did so.

Thirdly, I suspect they had grown tired of doing any manual memory management at all. Dropping explicit memory regions from the malloc() interface is a change that, on the surface, simplifies stuff even further. You make the implementation-side smarter and you don't have to worry about passing coremap or swapmap or anymap. Remember: the way programs and problems were approached didn't lead to complex object lifetimes. And when you had to deal with tangled lifetimes, malloc()/free() appear deceivably simple in the beginning.

That last point seems more "vibes" than evidence, but there is some evidence actually. In V7 they added galloc(3):

and Rob Pike had this in /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:15:

Ha, myth busted! The authors and people closest to C wanted garbage collection. Given how fast computers are -- and the pace of that -- this makes sense. It's even clearer if you look at what they did later with Limbo and Go. They wanted a higher level general purpose language to write programs in. They had C, so they tried to bolt GC on top of that.

Lastly, I should note that many of these problems were largely known, even at the time. In The Standard C library (1992), P. J. Plauger writes:

Allocating and freeing data objects on the heap in arbitrary order inevitably leaves unusable holes between some of the allocated data objects. That too lowers the usable size of the heap.

Don't overreact to this knowledge. Gather related data into a structure and allocate it all at once. That minimizes heap overhead, to be sure, but it is also good programming style. Do not gather unrelated data just to save heap overhead. Similarly, allocate data objects with similar lifetimes all at once, then free them at about the same time. That minimizes heap fragmentation, but it too is good style. Do not advance or defer unrelated heap operations just to minimize fragmentation. The storage allocation functions are an important aid to programming flexibility. Use them as they are intended to be used.

Criticism by yours truly: It's much easier to say "just do the right thing™" than show and provide tools for how to actually do it.

I don't know. Pay attention to good ideas, otherwise they might get lost? (literally in the case of V4, lol) Sounds cheesy.

Also, the "C object code improver" shatters the illusion that C was somehow magically fast. In fact, Ritchie later added an expression optimiser, and they kept extending both in each edition. I think C just wasn't slow, and it was made fast only with engineering effort put into the compiler (and even then, they had to add register because the compiler wasn't that smart either). It probably remained fast because Unix spread quickly and it carried C along with it, so hardware manufacturers adapted to C. There's a nice essay by Mike Pall discussing how modern CPUs try very hard to infer invariants from compiled C code (which the compiler tried very hard to optimise) and the costs associated with that.

At one point, I also want to investigate Inferno and Plan 9 more. Maybe the BSDs too. Until then...

(Kindly let me know if I made some mistake :)

Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

In robotics, price is basically actuator count. Stringman reaches an entire room with four motors, hanging its gripper from lines anchored in the ceiling corners. Working from above, it reaches floors too cluttered for any wheeled or legged robot. And since the lifting force is shared by all motors, payload capacity scales with their combined torque instead of a single actuator's, peaking near the center of the room where the lines share the load most evenly.

*0.75 m serial arm using the same DM-H6215 1 N·m direct drive actuators at rated torque, ignoring the weight of its own links. Stringman figure is for a 7 × 7 × 3 m room at the 28 N line tension limit, net of its 638 g gripper and marker.

Stringman is open source and OSHWA certified. The mechanical CAD, the PCBs, and the control software are all published.

We believe owners should be in control of their own robots. That's why Stringman can run air gapped on your local Wi-Fi network: the UI is served locally, AI models run on your own hardware, and no data ever leaves your network.

Give your home lab the capability of carrying parts from one workcell to another anywhere in the room, so you can get more out of your other robots. The Python API and MCP server is made for agents so you can get your workflow running right away.

2022 Porsche 911 GT3 RSR model by No Limits, CC BY 4.0, simplified. SO-101 arm from TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100, Apache 2.0.

Unlike desktop arms limited to a fixed radius, Stringman leverages a cable-driven architecture to access the full volume of a room. The work area volume per dollar of this type of robot is completely unmatched, all with fewer actuators than even the simplest mobile robots. Anchors and eylets are mounted in the corners of the room near the ceiling and define a four-sided work area within which any object can be moved from point to point.

That's roughly 500× the work area volume per dollar, at comparable 2 kg payload.

Secure the cleats to wall studs near the ceiling with wood screws, or to columns with ratchet straps.

Hang the anchors and connect the lines to the gripper.

Run calibration. This hands off process takes about five minutes and adapts Stringman to your room.

Step-by-step: picture guide or video guide

The original prototype was built in a room with a ceiling fan, and it still runs there today. Mount the anchors at or below the level of the blades and the lines can't physically reach it.

Several methods are available for control with default models for automatic grasping, target, and destination selection to make it easy to quickly build new behaviors.

Stringman is fully capable of LeRobot control using including Pi.05, JEPA, Multitask DiT, and others.

Collecting training data for new behaviors can be done from the UI, and as few as 50 episodes can be enough for certain models like DiT to learn a behavior.

As long as it remains installed, yes. However, when parked, they are up near the ceiling and out of the way. Clutter on the ceiling is preferable to clutter on the floor in our opinion. If you need to remove the anchors, they can be detached from their mounts without tools, leaving a relatively small white cleat on the wall.

Yes, it's just a matter of mounting the anchors at or below the level of the fan, making it physically impossible for the lines or marker tag to touch it. Similarly, the work area can be shrunk to exclude low hanging light fixtures if they are off to the side, but if the center of the room does contain low hanging objects, Stringman cannot be installed in that room.

When reaching a tension limit of 28 newtons (about the weight of a backpack), all motors relax and the lines can be pulled loose. Since they are overhead most of the time, it's uncommon for people to collide with them.

Not by default, but if you bind it with neufangled.com/playroom then you or anyone you share access with can operate it from anywhere, and access can be revoked at any time. Neufangled Robotics does not store any of the information from your robot that is forwarded through its servers.

For those who prefer to make the trade-off by binding their robot to an account, our web-based console allows you to monitor and control Stringman from anywhere. Think of it as a security camera with a hand.

If you do decide that you would like to make use of our cloud telemetry relay, You can use it, and still go back to a completely lan only mode whenever you want. Your data is never collected.

Organizing your home is a physical process, not a coding task. Use our clip-on fiducial tags to designate your laundry bin, toy box, and trash can. Stringman maps these locations visually. You don't need to tag individual pieces of clutter—just the destination. If there's something you never want it to pick up, you can mark that item as off-limits.

Networks trained to control stringman have learned that the word "toybox" refers to that tag, so you can use it to mark anything even if it doesn't look like the toyboxes from our training set.

You can also use the tags as arbitrary source and destination markers for ferry jobs, such as carrying items from one robot arm to another. or carrying laundry from the ground to a robotic folding station

A classroom with a Stringman robot gives your students a chance to become familiar with robotics fundamentals such as inverse kinematics, telemetry, and imitation learning while controlling an exotic and capable flying gripper. If you have walls and a MacBook, you're more than halfway there.

Cross embodiment is one of the biggest challenges in robotics, and showing that a model can operate a vastly different body type is a stronger result than moving it from one bimanual robot to another. Our datasets are public on Hugging Face, there's a controller-in-the-loop MuJoCo sim, and Stringman works with LeRobot, making it one of the most inexpensive robots to test on and a natural capstone project.

Mobile robots spend a significant portion of their time charging. Because Stringman is a powered from the wall, it's always ready for work. Furthermore, by removing the heavy battery pack, we've increased the payload capacity per dollar compared to mobile platforms that must waste energy carrying their own power supply.

The gripper's power is delivered via one of the support cables. A two-conductor FEP jacketed twisted pair cable with a tensile strength of 50N.

What's that pole for? Stringman's gripper hangs below the pivot point so it can reach the floor next to beds and tables. This additional linkage could allow unconstrained motion so Stringman employs active swing cancellation algorithms to counteract momentum, without adding the cost of any additional motors. This ensures the gripper remains steady and predictable even during rapid cross-room traversals.

There's a whole video about swing cancellation if you're curious about how it works!

Often, a simple solution that gets the job done has more value than a complex one. Stringman uses a two fingered gripper with a wrist. This is enough dexterity for the clutter it is designed to pick up, keeping weight and cost low and reliability high. In our household tests we have determined that more layers of grip tape is simply a better return on investment than more articulated fingers.

The gripper can rotate it's wrist to better place the fingers around flat sided or long objects.

For a easy preview of how it looks in your room, print the anchor mockup in white PLA and hold it up in a corner. Get the files.

TThe Stringman faceplate is easily swappable. Grab the STL or bambu 3MF files to print your faceplate in any color.

Join our community for support, live updates, and direct chat with the developer.

Watch full demonstrations, tutorials, and deep-dives into Stringman's kinematics and build processes.

Explore the open-source firmware, contribute to the codebase, and report technical issues.

Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

The car that I drive is a 2014 Renault Latitude. It's not a fancy car by any means and is starting to show its age, but it gets me from point A to point B and does everything else reasonably well so I've never really had any reason to complain.When I bought the car, the previous owner asked me whether I wanted a "navigation map SD card" with it.They mentioned that the car apparently needs this SD card just to change the time on the clock, but I didn't really find that believable - not that they were lying to me, but perhaps they couldn't figure out how to enter the correct settings menu. After all, videos of similar head units online showed the menu with the clock settings option right there.Since the maps on the SD card were apparently very out of date and didn't function properly, I decided I didn't need it and the previous owner tossed it.I didn't really miss it. The dashboard display did show a large "No maps found!" message taking up the majority of the display, but it didn't bother me too much.Like most other European countries, Estonia uses daylight saving time, and we recently switched from summer time (UTC+3) to "winter time" (UTC+2), which meant that the time displayed on the dashboard was out of sync by an hour. I dived into the settings menu, hoping to easily find the "Set time" option in there.That never happened.The menu where the "Set time" option should've been simply didn't have that option. I compared the menus with the ones in online videos, and the option was simply missing. There were two "Settings" buttons on the dash, and one of them worked but only let me change various Bluetooth and phonebook settings, with no time & date settings in sight. The second Settings button did not work whatsoever, instead showing a "No maps detected!" pop up message every time I pressed it.I must've spent an hour going through various menus, pressing various buttons or button combinations hoping to land in the correct menu, searching the web for information on this particular unit simply because I refused to believe that there was no option to change the time and I clearly must've been missing something obvious.Just RE itStill in denial, I decided to fetch the firmware and dig into it, hoping to find some indication on how to open the correct settings menu.Luckily, I wasn't the first to embark on this journey and someone had already done some reverse engineering work on this particular unit (https://github.com/andronedev/carminat-tomtom-live-re/blob/main/README.md). While it was in French and seemingly heavily LLM-assisted, it did point me to the correct URLs for fetching the update files themselves.When extracted, the update files included a ttsystem file which turned out to be an ext3 filesystem containing the device's root filesystem, which was pretty much exactly what I was looking for. The unit itself (TomTom Carminat LIVE, codename beaumont) is built around a Samsung S5P6440 SoC running TomTom's custom OS based on Linux 2.6.28.10.After reverse engineering it for a while, I came to the conclusion that the previous owner was completely correct. There was absolutely no way to enter the correct settings menu without a navigation SD card inserted. In fact, the menu definition pointing to the Settings applet was read from the SD card itself, and without one inserted containing the right menu definition, the unit didn't even know how to enter the Settings applet.This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me.What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. The system had DRM checks which rejected SD cards without the correct CID (a unique ID burned into the card) and files with signatures based on that specific CID, so I couldn't even copy the files to a blank SD card. I'm guessing the DRM was in place to prevent people from pirating maps.I don't want maps. I have a phone that I use for navigation. I just want to change the damn time.I checked online and found some third parties selling the card I presumably needed, but with shipping to Estonia, it would've cost me roughly 60 EUR, which I really didn't feel like paying.Fine. I'll just root it and do it myself.Easy wins?I couldn't find anyone online who'd jailbroken one of these before. I found some old forum threads with long-expired image links that had some pretty generic information about the unit itself and the general consensus was that it was difficult to root.I didn't expect a Linux 2.6 system from 2011 to be incredibly hard to hack, so I naively went in looking for some easy wins.My first idea was to modify the ext3 update image itself. It seemed like I could easily just mount the filesystem, modify some init scripts to do what I want, and copy it to a blank SD card for the unit to pick up my modified image and flash it.While the system showed confirmation prompts to install vanilla, unmodified ttsystem images with no problem, I could never get it to update to my modified image, and I had no idea why. I checked the updater logic present in the update file itself and couldn't see any reason why my image would be rejected.It was at this point that I set up an emulator with QEMU, a custom kernel also based on the same 2.6 version, some patches and a very simple CAN emulator for the system to actually boot - albeit reluctantly, wanting to reboot every 3 seconds, which I just patched out by ignoring reboot syscalls.I used this to test installing the modified update image in there. I then realized that I don't actually have the recovery partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing.Taking a closer look at the ttsystem image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could.Back to the drawing boardI'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved.For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system:rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro)Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard, and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi, which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal, which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec.This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011.Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script, a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time.I reversed ttn, the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed.More wild goose chasesI still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector.As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input.I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX/SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver, which launched whatever command line was provided with execve.This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh, which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec.The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.Among other things, I knew I could:Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfsWrite ASCII to paths of my own choosingThis is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there.core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, it turned out the unit doesn't really have a concept of timezones at all. It gets the time from GPS and stores the local offset as a number of minutes. Mine was set to 180.I changed it to 120.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

When I bought the car, the previous owner asked me whether I wanted a "navigation map SD card" with it.They mentioned that the car apparently needs this SD card just to change the time on the clock, but I didn't really find that believable - not that they were lying to me, but perhaps they couldn't figure out how to enter the correct settings menu. After all, videos of similar head units online showed the menu with the clock settings option right there.Since the maps on the SD card were apparently very out of date and didn't function properly, I decided I didn't need it and the previous owner tossed it.I didn't really miss it. The dashboard display did show a large "No maps found!" message taking up the majority of the display, but it didn't bother me too much.Like most other European countries, Estonia uses daylight saving time, and we recently switched from summer time (UTC+3) to "winter time" (UTC+2), which meant that the time displayed on the dashboard was out of sync by an hour. I dived into the settings menu, hoping to easily find the "Set time" option in there.That never happened.The menu where the "Set time" option should've been simply didn't have that option. I compared the menus with the ones in online videos, and the option was simply missing. There were two "Settings" buttons on the dash, and one of them worked but only let me change various Bluetooth and phonebook settings, with no time & date settings in sight. The second Settings button did not work whatsoever, instead showing a "No maps detected!" pop up message every time I pressed it.I must've spent an hour going through various menus, pressing various buttons or button combinations hoping to land in the correct menu, searching the web for information on this particular unit simply because I refused to believe that there was no option to change the time and I clearly must've been missing something obvious.Just RE itStill in denial, I decided to fetch the firmware and dig into it, hoping to find some indication on how to open the correct settings menu.Luckily, I wasn't the first to embark on this journey and someone had already done some reverse engineering work on this particular unit (https://github.com/andronedev/carminat-tomtom-live-re/blob/main/README.md). While it was in French and seemingly heavily LLM-assisted, it did point me to the correct URLs for fetching the update files themselves.When extracted, the update files included a ttsystem file which turned out to be an ext3 filesystem containing the device's root filesystem, which was pretty much exactly what I was looking for. The unit itself (TomTom Carminat LIVE, codename beaumont) is built around a Samsung S5P6440 SoC running TomTom's custom OS based on Linux 2.6.28.10.After reverse engineering it for a while, I came to the conclusion that the previous owner was completely correct. There was absolutely no way to enter the correct settings menu without a navigation SD card inserted. In fact, the menu definition pointing to the Settings applet was read from the SD card itself, and without one inserted containing the right menu definition, the unit didn't even know how to enter the Settings applet.This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me.What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. The system had DRM checks which rejected SD cards without the correct CID (a unique ID burned into the card) and files with signatures based on that specific CID, so I couldn't even copy the files to a blank SD card. I'm guessing the DRM was in place to prevent people from pirating maps.I don't want maps. I have a phone that I use for navigation. I just want to change the damn time.I checked online and found some third parties selling the card I presumably needed, but with shipping to Estonia, it would've cost me roughly 60 EUR, which I really didn't feel like paying.Fine. I'll just root it and do it myself.Easy wins?I couldn't find anyone online who'd jailbroken one of these before. I found some old forum threads with long-expired image links that had some pretty generic information about the unit itself and the general consensus was that it was difficult to root.I didn't expect a Linux 2.6 system from 2011 to be incredibly hard to hack, so I naively went in looking for some easy wins.My first idea was to modify the ext3 update image itself. It seemed like I could easily just mount the filesystem, modify some init scripts to do what I want, and copy it to a blank SD card for the unit to pick up my modified image and flash it.While the system showed confirmation prompts to install vanilla, unmodified ttsystem images with no problem, I could never get it to update to my modified image, and I had no idea why. I checked the updater logic present in the update file itself and couldn't see any reason why my image would be rejected.It was at this point that I set up an emulator with QEMU, a custom kernel also based on the same 2.6 version, some patches and a very simple CAN emulator for the system to actually boot - albeit reluctantly, wanting to reboot every 3 seconds, which I just patched out by ignoring reboot syscalls.I used this to test installing the modified update image in there. I then realized that I don't actually have the recovery partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing.Taking a closer look at the ttsystem image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could.Back to the drawing boardI'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved.For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system:rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro)Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard, and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi, which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal, which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec.This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011.Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script, a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time.I reversed ttn, the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed.More wild goose chasesI still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector.As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input.I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX/SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver, which launched whatever command line was provided with execve.This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh, which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec.The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.Among other things, I knew I could:Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfsWrite ASCII to paths of my own choosingThis is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there.core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, it turned out the unit doesn't really have a concept of timezones at all. It gets the time from GPS and stores the local offset as a number of minutes. Mine was set to 180.I changed it to 120.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.
